notes:
Here are the verse-by-verse notes for Psalm 107:23–43, drawn only from pages I could read. I ran out of research time before reaching some sources, so a few verses have thin notes.

**What I couldn't find**
- No netbible.org notes, and nothing from oca.org, catholic.com, lcms.org or 1517.org.
- No prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching on this passage.
- Verses 35–38 and 41–43 have little detailed material.
- The traditions don't split on doctrine here. The real difference is how to read it: as literal providence, as a picture of Israel's captivity, or as an allegory of the soul or the church.

---

## Section overview (vv. 23–32)
- Enduring Word (Guzik, Calvary Chapel) treats this as the last of four rescue scenes. Each follows the same pattern: people cry out in distress and God answers with deliverance. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-107/
- **The traditions differ on how to read it:**
  - *Methodist/Wesleyan:* Adam Clarke reads the storm as a figure of the exile: "This is the FOURTH comparison. Their captivity was as dangerous and alarming as a dreadful tempest at sea to a weather-beaten mariner." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/107-23.html
  - *Continental scholars:* Keil & Delitzsch, following Hengstenberg, insist it is "without any allegory" and is about real seafarers. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/107-23.html
  - *Reformed:* Calvin sees one more case of God's care over all people, likening rescued sailors to those raised "from the depth and darkness of the tomb". https://www.ccel.org/c/calvin/comment3/comm_vol11/htm/xvi.iv.htm

## v. 23
- Ellicott: "go down" fits Hebrew geography. From the Judean highlands it was a literal descent to the Mediterranean, just as Jonah "went down" to Joppa. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/107-23.html
- Spurgeon: Israelites sailed so rarely that sailors were surrounded with mystery, and their trade was seen as unusually daring and dangerous. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps107.cfm
- Pulpit Commentary: some Israelites did go to sea, as 1 Kings 9:26-28, 10:22, 22:48 and other passages show. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/107-23.htm
- Gill (Baptist): this is the fourth case of people in distress crying to the Lord, being helped, and so owing Him praise. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/107-23.html
- Keil & Delitzsch: the words point to trade, not fishing, as Luther correctly understood. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/107-23.htm
- Matthew Henry: people only went to sea on business (Solomon had no pleasure boat). Even so, those on lawful business may in faith place themselves under God's protection. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_107.cfm
- *Catholic (Augustine):* "great waters" means "among many peoples," since Revelation calls waters peoples. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801107.htm

## v. 24
- Benson (Methodist): the "works" may be creation, such as fish of many kinds, some huge, that other people never see. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/107-23.htm
- Calvin disagrees. He does not take it to mean the many wonders the ocean holds in general. For him the point is that sailors' lives are often in danger from storms. https://www.ccel.org/c/calvin/comment3/comm_vol11/htm/xvi.iv.htm
- Spurgeon agrees with Calvin: the main wonders are a sudden storm and the calm after it. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps107.cfm
- Augustine: "For what is deeper than human hearts?" https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801107.htm

## v. 25
- Spurgeon applies it to the soul: one word from God and the soul is in troubled waters, beset by many afflictions. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps107.cfm
- Another writer quoted by Spurgeon: God raises and stills the storm; worldly wise men stop at physical laws, but the Spirit sees the storm as God's work. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps107.cfm
- Augustine reads the storm as the church in trouble, with "storms of sedition, and dissensions" disturbing the ship. God wants both those who steer and those carried to cry to Him. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801107.htm

## v. 26
- Calvin, citing the Jewish commentator Kimchi: they are thrown up into the air, then tumble toward the ocean depths where they may drown. https://www.ccel.org/c/calvin/comment3/comm_vol11/htm/xvi.iv.htm
- Benson: the ships seem to touch the clouds, then sink as if buried, and passengers are ready to die of fear. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/107-23.html
- Augustine reads it inwardly: they rise "in daring" and sink "in fearing". https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801107.htm

## v. 27
- Spurgeon: they have tried every method navigation knows, and still cannot keep the ship afloat. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps107.cfm
- Calvin: when all human skill is baffled they give themselves up to wind and wave. His editor's notes give other translations, e.g. Horsley's "all their skill is drowned". https://www.ccel.org/c/calvin/comment3/comm_vol11/htm/xvi.iv.htm
- Keil & Delitzsch: their wisdom "swallowed itself up," consumed itself and came to nothing. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/107-29.htm
- Bob Utley (bible.org): the verb is literally "swallowed," used of sudden destruction, as when the sea swallows a ship. https://bible.org/seriespage/psalm-107
- Augustine applies it to church leaders: they seem wise when they speak and interpret, but in the storm all their wisdom is swallowed up. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801107.htm

## v. 28
- Spurgeon: God brought the trouble, so the sailors rightly turned to Him to remove it, and not in vain. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps107.cfm
- An older writer in Spurgeon's notes: storms bring to their knees those who would never kneel in a calm. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps107.cfm
- Augustine links it to Paul's trouble in Asia (2 Cor 1:8), where he was "pressed above strength". https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801107.htm

## v. 29
- Enduring Word: only God can calm the sea by command, which recalls Jesus calming the Sea of Galilee. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-107/
- Calvin: a secular writer would just say the winds died down, but this wording puts God's providence over everything. https://www.ccel.org/study/Psalm_107:30
- Barnes: God can also calm the soul's storm, the mind tossed by guilt and fear of judgment. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/107-29.htm
- Romaine (Anglican), quoted by Spurgeon: Christ is as almighty in the spiritual world as in nature and stills the soul's passions. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps107.cfm

## v. 30
- Spurgeon: the rougher the voyage, the more sailors long for port, and heaven becomes more and more "a desired haven". https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps107.cfm
- Biblical Illustrator: the haven suggests rest and safety. As long as Jehovah exists, the Christian soul is safe. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tbi/psalms-107.html

## vv. 31–32
- Enduring Word: the fourth and last refrain also calls people to exalt Him in the assembly of the people. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-107/
- Calvin: this thanks should be praised in great assemblies, not just privately or in the family. Elders are named because the wiser and more experienced are better able to hear and witness this praise. https://www.ccel.org/study/Psalm_107:30

## vv. 33–34
- Enduring Word: God can change land from good to bad when the goal is judging the wicked. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-107/
- Gill: this means well-watered land like the area around Sodom, or Canaan, turned into desert by God's judgment. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/lsv/psalms/107-33.html
- Barnes: "barrenness" is literally "saltness" in Hebrew, because salty soil is barren, as around the Dead Sea. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/asv/psalms/107-34.html
- Matthew Henry: "If the land be bad, it is because the inhabitants are so." https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_107.cfm
- Benson: God punishes sin in some this way and so prevents it in others. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/107-33.htm
- Clarke: here the psalmist moves from the captivity to how God generally treats the poor and needy and opposes their oppressors. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/107-33.html
- *Modern scholarship:* Coffman reports that Mitchell Dahood (Anchor Bible) applied these verses to the Canaanites driven out for their sin. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/107-34.html
- *Caution:* Bible Hub quotes an older writer, not named in my results, who applies the verse to the Jewish synagogue as "cursed with infidelity" after Christ's death. It's a dated reading you may want to mention only as such. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/107-33.htm

## vv. 35–38
- Enduring Word: dry land can become places of fruitfulness and civilization. The psalmist relied on God to bless the land when the people returned to it. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-107/
- Bible Hub summary: God settles the hungry so they "multiply greatly," able to reverse the fortunes of peoples and lands. https://biblehub.com/psalms/107.htm

## v. 39
- Keil & Delitzsch: their prosperity drew the envy of tyrants, but God ended the tyranny and restored His people. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/107-40.htm

## v. 40
- Pulpit Commentary: a direct quotation of Job 12:21, which does not make it spurious. Hengstenberg: wandering in a pathless waste means helpless embarrassment. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/107-40.htm
- Barnes: God treats princes like common people. The word for "waste" is tôhû, meaning wasteness or emptiness. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/107-40.htm
- Gill offers two readings: exiled rulers wandering like Nebuchadnezzar, or (with Aben Ezra and Kimchi) rulers whose wisdom is confused. He also applies it to "antichristian princes" in Revelation 16. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/107-40.htm
- Geneva Bible notes (Reformed): for their tyranny God makes their subjects despise them. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/107-40.htm
- Calvin: when God throws rulers down, people wake up and pay attention to His judgments. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/107-39.html
- Matthew Henry: "Let not princes be envied, nor the poor despised", since God can change both. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_107.cfm

## v. 41
- Keil & Delitzsch: "families like a flock" means families grow until they look like a large, lively flock. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/107-40.htm
- Enduring Word: as God turns desert into pools, He lifts the poor far from affliction. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-107/
- Bible Hub links the reversal theme to Hannah's song (1 Samuel 2:7–8). https://biblehub.com/psalms/107.htm
- Matthew Henry: God should be acknowledged both in founding families and building them up. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/107-40.html

## v. 42
- Enduring Word: the righteous are glad that God brings down the proud and lifts the poor. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-107/
- Matthew Henry: they rejoice in God's attributes being glorified and His rule over people shown. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_107.cfm

## v. 43
- Enduring Word: the psalm ends as a wisdom psalm. The wise watch how God works in history and so grasp His lovingkindness through His acts, not just in words. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-107/
- Bible Hub: v. 43 resembles Hosea 14:9. https://biblehub.com/psalms/107.htm
- A note on the Bible Hub commentary page says the wise learn from this psalm man's weakness and God's power and kindness, given for His mercy's sake, not our merit. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/107-33.htm
